outcome: The L1 (l_1^d) case has moved once since 26 January 2024: Gallinger (Zenodo preprint, 27 September 2026, Lean-formalised per its author) claims e(l_1^5)=10 and e(l_1^6)=12, extending the pre-2024 cases d<=4; the general case d>=7 remains open, and the other 2026 preprints concern the l_p (p not 1) half of Kusner's conjecture.
problem_asks: (1) For every dimension d, every equilateral set in d-dimensional L1 space (R^d with the l_1 norm) has at most 2d points: e(l_1^d) <= 2d. (2) Since the cross-polytope {±e_i} gives 2d equidistant points, the bullet's full content is e(l_1^d) = 2d exactly, for every d. Interpretation: 'L1 spaces' is read as the finite-dimensional l_1^d, as the 2d bound requires. The bullet does not ask about the l_p, p>1, half of Kusner's conjecture (n+1 points for 1<p<infinity), which many 2026 results address; those are recorded below as out of scope.

events.what_happened: Bandelt, Chepoi and Laurent, 'Embedding into rectilinear spaces', Discrete & Computational Geometry 19 (1998) 595-604, showed e(l_1^3)=6, i.e. the 2d value for d=3. Known from the Wikipedia 'Equilateral dimension' citation and two secondary summaries (a Minkowski-geometry survey and a 2020 arXiv paper); the primary paper was not opened.
events.delivers: e(l_1^3)=6, i.e. the conjectured value for d=3 (cross-polytope lower bound plus matching upper bound). Covers dimension 3 only.
events.remains: The exact value 2d for every d >= 4.

checked_by.what_they_did: Accepted the paper for publication; referee reports not seen

events.direction: Consistent with the conjecture (value 2d) at d=3.

events.what_happened: Koolen, Laurent and Schrijver, 'Equilateral dimension of the rectilinear space', Designs, Codes and Cryptography 21 (2000) 149-164, showed e(l_1^4)=8, i.e. the 2d value for d=4. A CWI report with the same title (ir.cwi.nl/pub/1171) appeared in search results; its date was not established and it was not opened. The 2000 date comes from the Wikipedia citation and a search summary; the journal paper was not opened.
events.delivers: e(l_1^4)=8, i.e. the conjectured value for d=4. Covers dimension 4 only.
events.remains: The exact value 2d for every d >= 5.

events.direction: Consistent with the conjecture (value 2d) at d=4.

events.what_happened: Alon and Pudlak, 'Equilateral sets in l_p^n', Geometric and Functional Analysis 13 (2003) 467-482, proved for p=1 that e(l_1^n) <= c*n*log n for an absolute constant c. Known from the Wikipedia citation and secondary summaries of the 2003 paper; the primary paper was not opened.
events.delivers: An upper bound on e(l_1^n) of order n log n for every n. Does not determine whether the value is 2n.
events.remains: The exact value 2n for every d; only an order-of-magnitude upper bound is established.

events.direction: Does not cut either way on 2d: the bound is far above 2d for large d.

events.what_happened: Swanepoel, 'A problem of Kusner on equilateral sets', arXiv math/0309317 (v1 19 Sep 2003; v2 7 Sep 2006), published Archiv der Mathematik 83 (2004) 164-170. Addresses the other half of Kusner's question (the n+1 claim for l_p^n): proves it for p=4 and any d, and shows it fails for 1<p<2 with d large. Discarded for this bullet: the question is about l_p with p not 1, and the abstract does not mention p=1.
events.revisions: v2 7 Sep 2006 (comment: 'Small correction to Proposition 2.'); journal version Arch. Math. 83 (2004) 164-170.
events.delivers: For l_p^d with 1<p<2 and large d, the n+1 claim fails; for p=4 it holds for all d. Nothing about p=1.
events.remains: Everything the bullet asks: the l_1 value e(l_1^d)=2d for all d.

checked_by.what_they_did: Published the paper (2004); referee reports not seen

events.direction: Concerns the l_p, p not 1, half of Kusner's conjecture; disproves the n+1 claim for some 1<p<2. No bearing on the l_1 value.

events.what_happened: Aaron Lin, 'Equilateral sets in the l_1 sum of Euclidean spaces', arXiv:1811.04783 (submitted 12 Nov 2018, one version). Constructs equilateral sets of size at least dimension+1 in E^a (+)_1 E^b for a<=27 and some other pairs. Discarded for this bullet: the space is an l_1 sum of Euclidean spaces, not l_1^d, and the page does not mention Kusner's conjecture.
events.delivers: Lower bounds of size a+b+1 in the l_1 sum E^a (+)_1 E^b. Says nothing about e(l_1^d).

events.what_happened: Ge, Xu and Zhou, 'Kusner's conjecture: exact values and linear bounds', arXiv:2606.03987 (submitted 2 June 2026; v1 only). Main results are for l_p^n: the n+1 claim for 2<=p<=4 in every dimension; for p in [4k+2, 4k+4] an upper bound (2k+1)n+1; on the complementary intervals an O_p(n log n) bound. The paper also treats the torus T^n. For l_1^n, the abstract states the conjectured value 2n for p=1 but the paper does not claim to prove it; its intro gives an n log(2n)-order bound for 1<=p<2 (Theorem 1.3 with k=0, as I read it), which covers p=1.
events.revisions: v1 only (2 June 2026) per arXiv listing.
events.delivers: For l_1^n: an n log(2n) upper bound, of the same order as Alon-Pudlak 2003; I could not establish whether the constant or the log factor is improved. For l_p with 2<=p<=4: the n+1 claim in full (the other half of Kusner's conjecture, out of scope for this bullet).
events.remains: The exact value e(l_1^d)=2d for every d; the paper gives only an n log(2n) bound for l_1.
events.direction: For l_1: no bearing on the value 2d, only an order-of-magnitude bound. For the l_p half: proves the n+1 claim for 2<=p<=4; the later Chalmers and Xiong counterexamples lie outside that range, so no conflict.

events.what_happened: L. R. Chalmers (University of Otago), 'A counterexample to Kusner's conjecture on equilateral sets', arXiv:2608.14013 (v1 14 August 2026; v2 5 September 2026). Gives 58 pairwise-equidistant points in l_5^56, so e(l_5^56) >= 58 > 57, for the l_p (p=5) n+1 claim; the construction holds on an open interval of exponents around 5. Accompanied by a Zenodo certificate and verifier (DOI 10.5281/zenodo.21911503; Zenodo lists v3 dated 13 August 2026). Discarded for this bullet: p=5, not p=1.
events.revisions: v2 5 September 2026 (author's comment: amended to reduce reliance on supplemental material and to specify the search method).
events.delivers: A counterexample to the l_p n+1 claim at p=5 (n=56). Nothing about l_1.
events.directly_checkable: The 58-point configuration: the Zenodo record holds integer certificate arrays (certificate_data.npz) and verify.py, which checks six certificate inequalities in exact integer arithmetic; plain Python, with python-flint for speed. I did not run the verifier.
events.direction: Against the l_p n+1 claim at p=5. No bearing on l_1.
events.object: 58 points in R^56 with all pairwise l_5 distances equal. Found by minimising a scale-invariant equidistance residual and then removing points and coordinates; certified by a contraction argument in exact integer arithmetic on a rational box of radius 2^-33, whose unique fixed point is an exact zero with positive common distance. Explicit as a certificate, computer-found, not a closed-form construction. (Description from a WebFetch summary of the HTML, not checked against the page text.)

events.what_happened: Nathan Xiong, 'Kusner's conjecture is false for p>4', arXiv:2609.14794 (v1, submitted 13 September 2026, sole author). For each p>4 defines m=m(p) and constructs an equilateral set of 8m points in R^(8m-2) in l_p, disproving the n+1 claim for those p. States that together with Swanepoel (1<p<2) and Ge-Xu-Zhou (2<=p<=4) the conjecture is 'resolved for all 1<p<infinity'. Discarded for this bullet: p>4, not p=1. The acknowledgements say the construction was found by an AI model (see ai).
events.delivers: A counterexample to the l_p n+1 claim for every p>4. Nothing about p=1.
events.time_since_posted: about 4 weeks (since 13 September 2026); MathWorld states that as of 22 September 2026 no independent specialist review had been reported.
events.doubts: Single-author preprint about four weeks old with no reported review (MathWorld, as of 22 September 2026). Nothing specific to the l_1 bullet.
events.direction: Against the l_p n+1 claim for every p>4. No bearing on l_1.
events.object: An equilateral set of 8m points in R^(8m-2) under the l_p metric, built from Hadamard matrices H_k and H_(k+2) with front and back coordinate blocks and a parameter a that is shown to exist by an intermediate-value argument (Lemma 4.2); distances are checked in four cases. The set is explicit once m(p) is fixed; the existence of a is non-constructive. (Description from a WebFetch summary of the HTML, not checked against the page text.)

events.what_happened: Drew Gallinger (University of Toronto), 'Kusner's Conjecture in l_1^5 and l_1^6', Zenodo preprint DOI 10.5281/zenodo.22984024 (v1, created 27 September 2026, CC BY 4.0). Abstract: 'We prove the next two cases, e(l_1^5)=10, e(l_1^6)=12', citing Bandelt-Chepoi-Laurent for n<=3 and Koolen-Laurent-Schrijver for n=4. Method per the abstract: 'a geometric clipping reduction with reciprocal weighted energy identities' plus two estimates, reducing the problem to the exclusion of a two-parameter scalar region. The record says 'Both results are formally verified in Lean' and links github.com/kusner-l1/kusnerl1-lean (Lean 4, Apache-2.0; one commit, author date 26 September 2026 15:04 UTC, message 'Initialize Kusner L1 formalization'; the README says the formalisation 'predates later revisions and will be updated and reverified for the final paper'). The PDF could not be read by me.
events.revisions: v1 only. README says the formalisation will be updated and reverified for the final paper.
events.delivers: e(l_1^5)=10 and e(l_1^6)=12 per the abstract; with the cited pre-2024 results, the 2d value for every d <= 6. The Lean theorem equilateralDimension_eq is stated for 2 <= n <= 6. Restricted to d = 5 and d = 6 as new cases.

summary: Since 26 January 2024 the l_1 case has moved once, and that movement rests on a single unreviewed preprint. Gallinger (Zenodo, posted 27 September 2026) claims e(l_1^5)=10 and e(l_1^6)=12, extending the pre-2024 cases d<=4 (Bandelt-Chepoi-Laurent 1998 for d=3; Koolen-Laurent-Schrijver 2000 for d=4). The Zenodo record says both results are formally verified in Lean, and links a GitHub repository (kusner-l1/kusnerl1-lean, one commit dated 26 September 2026). I read the Lean definitions and theorem statements: equilateralDimension is the supremum of encard over equilateral sets in L1 n, in ℕ∞; equilateralDimension_eq covers 2<=n<=6, and equilateralDimension_five and _six are its instances. Three of the imported files contain no sorry. But the general upper-bound lemma is conditional on an exclusion hypothesis, and I could not confirm that it is discharged for n=5 and n=6: Averaging.lean, Audit.lean, and the L1 and UnitEquilateral definitions were not read. The PDF holding the proof could not be read through the fetch tool, so the proof, its method beyond the abstract's one-line description, and any acknowledgement are unverified by me. The Wikipedia 'Equilateral dimension' article, edited 27 September 2026, cites Gallinger and states the value as known for d<=6; that is a citing statement, not a verification. My searches found no public expert engagement with Gallinger. The 2026 results that drew attention concern the l_p half of Kusner's conjecture, not this bullet. Ge-Xu-Zhou (2 June 2026) prove the n+1 claim for 2<=p<=4; for p=1 in R^n they give an n log(2n) bound of the same order as Alon-Pudlak 2003, and I could not establish that it improves that bound. Chalmers (14 August 2026) gives 58 equidistant points in l_5^56, and Xiong (13 September 2026) gives a construction for every p>4; both are outside the bullet. Chalmers's paper credits 'OpenAI's GPT-5.6 Sol' with help implementing the search and drafting; Xiong's credits 'OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra model' with finding the construction. These quotes come from WebFetch summaries of the HTML pages, not from checked page text. Neither names an AI system for an l_1 result, and no AI attribution appears in the readable parts of the Gallinger record, repository, or commit list. MathWorld's summary of Xiong says the construction was credited to GPT-6 Astra and that no independent review was reported as of 22 September 2026. Close calls, both readings: (1) whether a Lean-verified, single-author Zenodo deposit counts as a result in the bullet's sense is for the judging pass; I record it as an event with its signals. (2) n=5 and n=6 are a restricted case of a bullet that asks for every d; the bullet remains open for d>=7 on either reading. (3) The Ge-Xu-Zhou p=1 bound is recorded as an order-n log n bound; whether it is new is unresolved. A search snippet also mentioned an undated Society for Science abstract on l_1 'graph rigidity' saying the conjecture is not known beyond n=4; the PDF was unreadable, so I cannot say whether it predates or postdates Gallinger, or whether it is a claim.
competing_reading: Read strictly, the bullet asks for e(l_1^d)=2d for every d, and Gallinger settles only d=5 and d=6, so the bullet stays open and the Wikipedia phrase 'known to be exactly 2d for d<=6' overstates the evidence. The stronger reading: a machine-checked proof of two new cases is a resolution of two sub-cases the bullet names implicitly, which moves the l_1 quantity the bullet asks for; the Lean record makes it stronger evidence than a bare preprint. What would weaken or strengthen it is whether the exclusion step is discharged in Lean for n=5 and 6, not the number of readers so far.
what_would_settle_it: (1) A readable copy of the Gallinger PDF: the proof of the n=5 and n=6 cases, its method, and its acknowledgements or contribution statement (for any AI system). (2) Confirmation that equilateralDimension_eq for n=5 and n=6 uses no open exclusion hypothesis: the Averaging.lean and ScalarReduction.lean proofs for those n, and the Audit.lean output. (3) The Lean definitions of L1 and UnitEquilateral, to check they match the problem's equal-distance condition in the l_1 norm. (4) Any journal acceptance or named expert reading of Gallinger. (5) The 'final paper' version the README promises, and whether its statement changes. (6) The acknowledgements of the Ge-Xu-Zhou full text (the final 50,307 characters of the HTML were not read) and of Xiong's and Chalmers's full texts, to confirm what AI involvement they disclose.
